assumptions: Injury mechanism can be external mechanical force or penetration
Normal function is the baseline against which disruption is judged
primitives.breakdown_regime: Applies to traumatic causes only; non traumatic brain dysfunction is outside this definition

layer2.mapping: Definition as an event classifier: a reasoning engine must first classify whether an observed disruption has a traumatic mechanism before applying any TBI trajectory, separating mechanism from severity and from outcome
layer2.telemetry: Mechanism of injury, head impact history, presentation setting

reasoning_traces.think:
This report is a federal synthesis about a medical and educational problem, and its machinery is worth reading as a reasoning system rather than as a list of facts. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, working with the National Institutes of Health and a broad writing group, set out to describe how traumatic brain injury affects children in the United States, what happens to those children over time, what systems are supposed to help them, and where those systems fail. The core move in the report is to treat childhood brain injury as a trajectory problem. An injury happens at a point in development, and development does not stop. The child keeps growing into new cognitive, social, and physical demands, and the injury interacts with every later demand. That single framing explains most of the report structure. Severity is classified at presentation, but the report repeatedly warns that presentation is not destiny. Mild injuries usually resolve in weeks, and the report gives a concrete decay curve for symptom persistence, yet a meaningful minority of mild cases still need school support a year later, and deficits from more serious injuries may not become visible until the child reaches the developmental stage that requires the damaged function. A reasoning engine that closes a case at discharge, or that treats an early normal check as proof of full recovery, will systematically miss exactly the cases this report is about.
The second piece of machinery is stratification. Almost every quantity in the report is conditional. Burden is conditional on age, because causes differ by age and because entry into care differs by age and insurance. Disability is conditional on severity, with a sharp gradient between mild and moderate to severe injury. Recovery is conditional on family functioning, socioeconomic resources, co occurring conditions, and pre injury functioning. School outcomes are conditional on severity and on whether the school ever learns that an injury occurred. Even the count of cases is conditional on the observation channel, because most mild cases first appear in primary care rather than emergency departments, and some never appear in care at all. The report therefore teaches a discipline: never quote an unconditional number when the source gives a conditional one, and never build a projection from a single channel count without asking what that channel misses. That discipline transfers directly to any prediction system that ingests surveillance style data.
The third piece is systems analysis. Children with brain injury are served, or failed, by at least two large systems that do not share records: healthcare and education. Healthcare identifies and treats the acute injury and then, in most cases, discharges the child home with no formal long term monitoring. Education is where the child spends the day, where cognitive and behavioral changes are most visible, and where supports such as special education, Section 504 accommodations, and early intervention are delivered, but education often never receives the injury information, and children are identified for services at rates far below what incidence and disability figures imply. The report names this as under identification and treats it as a measurable gap between need and receipt. Around those two systems sit state lead agencies, trust funds, federal grant programs, family support centers, and rehabilitation facilities, each with its own eligibility rules and geographic variation. The report is blunt that coordination work, when systems do not do it, falls on parents, who are suddenly required to advocate in two bureaucracies while also coping with changes in their child and strain in the family. Family functioning then feeds back into child outcomes, which closes a loop: system fragmentation raises family burden, and family burden worsens the very outcomes the systems exist to improve.
The fourth piece is an honest account of evidence. For mild injury, the report describes the development of the first evidence based federal guideline, built from systematic review and expert workgroup judgment, with pacing and graduated return to cognitive and physical activity as a central recommendation. For moderate and severe injury, it states plainly that standards are weak, that individualized symptom management is the common practice in the absence of evidence, and that management overall has rested more on consensus and clinical experience than on rigorous trials. It also lists what research is missing: true incidence, developmental timing effects, recovery trajectories by age and severity, the separate contributions of family environment and co occurring conditions, and evaluations of the care models themselves. A reasoning engine should take that as an instruction about confidence. Some quantities in this report are measured rates from defined studies. Others are expert consensus. Others are identified unknowns. Treating all three at the same confidence level would corrupt any downstream reasoning.
For a sports and health reasoning engine, the value of this report is not a set of betting inputs and the report contains no such inputs. Its value is structural. It supplies base rates and conditional rates for a real injury domain, a validated recovery time course for mild injury, a model of latent deficit emergence tied to developmental demand, a worked example of observation channel bias, and a map of how handoffs between systems lose information and outcomes. Those are general reasoning templates. Base rates must be age and severity conditioned. Trajectories must be projected forward to the next demand, not just to the next check in. Observation channels must be audited for what they miss. Handoffs must be treated as loss points. Family and social context must be carried as variables that modify outcomes, not as background color. Where the report breaks is also instructive. Its counts are anchored in 2012 and 2013 data published in 2018, so absolute numbers will drift. Several key rates come from single studies with specific definitions, especially disability defined as service use, which confounds impairment with access. Long term adult outcomes are acknowledged to be thinly studied, and there are no equations, no fitted models, and no individual level prediction rules in the report at all. Anyone who needs a quantitative forecast must build it elsewhere and use this report for structure, priors, and sanity checks.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage of this report runs through the Traumatic Brain Injury Act, first enacted in 1996 and reauthorized in 2008 and 2014, which directed the CDC to study brain injury management in children and to report to Congress. Behind that statute sits decades of pediatric rehabilitation work, including Mark Ylvisaker and colleagues in the 1980s, who first framed childhood head injury rehabilitation around the developing child rather than the injured adult, and a long line of longitudinal outcome studies from researchers in Cincinnati, Columbus, Houston, and elsewhere who followed injured children into school and adolescence. The report also inherits the concussion awareness wave of the 2000s and 2010s, state return to play laws in all fifty states, and the federal special education framework built by the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act and Section 504, which together created the school side of the care system the report evaluates.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors write for Congress, agency leaders, clinicians, educators, and state program staff at the same time, and they model the reader as a decision maker who controls systems rather than individual cases. Their model of the domain is ecological: a child develops inside a family, a school, a healthcare system, and a state service landscape, and injury outcomes are produced by that whole ecology, not by the lesion alone. They assume the reader may still think of brain injury as an emergency department event, so they work to replace that picture with a chronic, developmental, cross system picture. They also assume goodwill but fragmented responsibility, which is why so many recommendations are about communication, identification, monitoring, and training rather than about a single new treatment.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: This work vetoes several tempting simplifications in any layered reasoning system. It vetoes closing an injury case at acute discharge, because it documents late emerging deficits and the absence of long term monitoring. It vetoes treating mild severity as equivalent to no consequence, because it quantifies school support need a year after mild injury. It vetoes single channel incidence counts, because it shows most mild cases enter outside the emergency department. It vetoes attributing outcomes to injury biology alone, because it establishes family functioning, socioeconomic context, and co occurring conditions as determinants. And it vetoes confident protocol claims for moderate and severe injury, because it states that the evidence base there is thin and practice is individualized.

universal_lens: Any injury or shock to a still developing system should be reasoned about as a trajectory interruption, not a one time event. Effects can stay hidden until later growth creates the demand that reveals them, observed counts depend on which channel you watch, outcomes are modified by the family and resource context around the individual, and when two institutions share responsibility without sharing information, the gap between need and service becomes the main measurable failure. That template applies to development, organizations, infrastructure, and learning systems far beyond medicine.
gsi_mapping: The Galaxy Sports Institute takes from this report a rigorous injury and recovery framework for youth sport: age and severity conditioned base rates, a quantified mild injury recovery time course, the principle that deficits can emerge when new demands arrive, and a systems view in which school, family, and medical care must exchange information for a young athlete to be supported. It also takes a research agenda discipline: name the unknowns, separate measured rates from consensus, and build monitoring where none exists, rather than assuming discharge means resolution.
gse_mapping: The Galaxy Sports Edge reasoning engine takes structural value only, with no betting content: conditional base rates instead of pooled averages, trajectory projection to the next demand point instead of a single snapshot, observation channel auditing so a count from one source is treated as a lower bound, handoff loss modeling between systems, and context variables such as family and socioeconomic resources carried as genuine modifiers of outcomes. Applied to athlete health reasoning, it supports more honest availability and recovery reasoning, explicit uncertainty where evidence is consensus rather than measured, and refusal to treat a mild label or an early clearance as proof that nothing follows.
